content.title: About
content.content: Dirty rice is a classic Creole dish from Louisiana, consisting of rice sautéed with ground meat (often turkey, beef or pork), browned offal, green onions, and a blend of spices. The name comes from the dark color the dish acquires from the blood and browned organ meats, giving it a rich, savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the 19th‑century African‑American communities of Louisiana, using inexpensive organ meats.
The word “dirty” refers to the color, not to the quality of the food.
Many variations exist: turkey, chicken, shrimp, or even a vegetarian version with mushrooms.
Dirty rice is commonly served as a side to fried meats, seafood, or Creole soups.
Traditional recipes often included blood sausage, intensifying the “dirty” hue.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat and offal provide a substantial amount of complete protein, essential for tissue repair and growth.

items.title: Rich source of iron
items.content: Blood‑rich organ meats contain heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole‑grain rice supply B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber from rice
items.content: Rice, especially when whole‑grain, adds fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The dish contains no added sugars, making it suitable for moderate‑carb diets.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Traditional recipes often use soy sauce or generous salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Cholesterol levels
items.content: Offal and fatty meats can raise cholesterol if consumed frequently.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp or crab versions may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improperly cooked organ meats may harbor pathogens; thorough cooking is essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve dirty rice hot as a main dish or as a side to fried meats, fish, or Creole soups. Garnish with fresh parsley or green onions and add a dash of hot sauce if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, portion into containers and freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet with cheese and dark‑green vegetables, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet prepared without added fat, enriched with cream cheese and dark‑green vegetables (spinach, broccoli, kale). Eggs provide high‑quality protein, while the vegetables add vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs contain all essential amino acids in optimal proportions.
Cream cheese adds calcium and a modest amount of fat, but in moderate amounts it does not significantly raise the dish’s calorie count.
Dark‑green vegetables are rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, supporting eye health.
Cooking without oil preserves the natural flavors of the ingredients and reduces total calories.
Traditional omelets are often fried in butter, whereas this recipe relies on the egg’s own fat.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: One serving provides about 6 g of complete protein, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply vitamin B12, riboflavin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from cheese
items.content: Cream cheese contributes calcium for bone health and a small amount of vitamin D.

items.title: Antioxidants from green vegetables
items.content: Lutein, zeaxanthin, and vitamin K support vision and cardiovascular health.

items.title: Low added‑fat content
items.content: Omitting oil reduces overall calories and saturated fat intake.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs or milk proteins may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium in cheese
items.content: Cream cheese can be salty, so choose a low‑sodium version if you need to limit salt intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat the eggs with a splash of water, stir in grated cream cheese and finely chopped green vegetables. Pour the mixture into a pre‑heated non‑stick pan and cook over medium heat, gently lifting the edges until the omelet sets. Serve immediately.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a non‑stick pan without adding oil.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen yogurt bar, chocolate is a frozen yogurt bar coated with a chocolate glaze. The combination of smooth yogurt and crunchy chocolate makes it a popular snack for both children and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yogurt base contains live probiotic cultures that support gut health.
The chocolate coating is often made from dark chocolate, increasing antioxidant content.
Frozen yogurt bars first appeared in the United States in the 1970s as a lighter alternative to ice cream.
Flavor is frequently enhanced with natural aromatics such as vanilla or berries.
Bars are packaged in individual wrappers, facilitating transport and storage.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Live cultures in the yogurt help maintain a healthy digestive microbiome.

items.title: Lower Fat Content
items.content: Compared with traditional ice cream, frozen yogurt bars usually contain less fat.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Yogurt provides a good source of calcium for strong bones.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Chocolate Antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate is rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Milk Protein Allergy
items.content: Yogurt contains lactose and casein, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Bars are often sweetened, so people monitoring sugar intake should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Thermal Shock
items.content: If the bar warms too quickly, the chocolate coating may crack, affecting texture.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Yogurt’s low pH can be irritating to sensitive teeth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bar straight from the freezer, allowing the chocolate coating to soften slightly. It can also be sliced and added to fruit salads or smoothies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bars at –18 °C or lower in a sealed package. After removal from the freezer, consume within 30 minutes for optimal texture. Do not keep thawed bars for more than 2 hours.

potato-mashed-from-dry-mix-nfs.title: Potato, mashed, from dry mix, NFS

content.title: About
content.content: The dry mix for mashed potatoes (NFS) provides a convenient way to obtain smooth mash without boiling and mashing fresh potatoes. The mix typically contains dehydrated potato, salt, spices, and sometimes dry dairy ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry mash mixes are widely used in cafeterias and catering to speed up preparation.
Modern drying technology preserves much of the flavor and texture of fresh potatoes.
The formulation may include additives such as dry cream or milk powder to enhance creaminess.
The mix is shelf‑stable, requiring no refrigeration and having a long shelf life.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The mix provides complex carbs that deliver sustained energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It retains vitamin B6 and B3, important for metabolism.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, supporting heart and muscle function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike mash made with butter, the dry mix is low in fat unless added during cooking.

items.title: Convenience
items.content: Quick preparation saves time, which is beneficial for busy schedules.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some mixes contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Dairy or gluten may be present; check the label if you have allergies.

items.title: Nutrient loss
items.content: Prolonged storage can degrade certain vitamins, so freshness matters.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Combine the mix with hot water or milk in the ratios indicated on the package, stir vigorously until smooth, and serve hot. Optional additions include butter, cheese, or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry mix in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within a few months for best quality.

summer-squash-yellow-or-green-fresh-cook.title: Summer squash, yellow or green, fresh, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash (Cucurbita pepo) is the immature fruit of the squash plant, usually yellow or green. Fresh fruits are tender, juicy, and have a mild flavor. Cooking them in butter or margarine preserves their natural sweetness and gives a silky texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belongs to the cucurbit family, close to zucchini, pumpkins, and cucumbers.
Unlike many vegetables, both the flesh and the skin of summer squash are edible.
Yellow varieties arise from natural genetic variation, not from added colorants.
They are used worldwide: in Italy for ratatouille, in Japan for tempura, and in the US for fried sticks.
Fresh summer squash is about 95 % water, so it loses moisture quickly if stored too long.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: With only about 17 kcal per 100 g, summer squash is an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to cucurbit vegetables.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic squash, wash thoroughly to remove possible chemical residues.

items.title: Nutrient loss with over‑cooking
items.content: Excessive high‑heat cooking can degrade heat‑sensitive vitamins, especially vitamin C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Summer squash can be sautéed, stewed, roasted, or steamed. Cooking it in butter or margarine adds a rich flavor and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins. Slice into cubes or rounds, add to stews, omelets, pasta dishes, or serve as a simple side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store summer squash in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container, where it stays fresh for up to 5 days. Keep it away from ethylene‑producing fruits, which accelerate ripening. Rinse under running water before cooking.

taco-corn-tortilla-pork-with-beans-chees.title: Corn Tortilla Taco with Pork, Beans and Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A corn tortilla taco filled with pork, beans and cheese is a classic Mexican dish. The thin corn tortilla is lightly toasted, while the juicy pork, seasoned beans and melted cheese create a balanced, flavorful bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn tortillas have been used in Mexico for over 7,000 years.
Pork for tacos is often marinated in a blend of chili, lime and spices for a distinctive aroma.
Beans are a traditional source of plant protein in Mexican cuisine, commonly served as refried beans.
Cheese used in tacos is often queso fresco or melted cheddar.
Traditional serving method is to fold the tortilla in half and eat it by hand.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pork and beans provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Beans contain soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pork supplies vitamin B12, while beans are a good source of folate, both important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Corn tortilla and beans deliver iron, magnesium and potassium.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Corn tortillas have a lower glycemic index than wheat flour tortillas, helping to moderate blood sugar spikes.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn products, including tortillas.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese and sauces can increase sodium intake, which should be monitored by people with hypertension.

items.title: Fat content of meat
items.content: Pork can contain saturated fats; choosing lean cuts or trimming excess fat is recommended.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Traditional tacos are calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hold the taco in one hand, folding the tortilla in half. Add fresh toppings such as diced tomatoes, onion, cilantro and a squeeze of lime for extra brightness. Serve with salsa, guacamole or sour cream if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared tacos in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Keep tortillas in a dry place; if they become soft, briefly warm them on a dry skillet before serving.
